Yitzhak Rabin. On November 4, 1995, the Israeli Prime Minister was shot and killed by Yigal Amir, a right-wing Israeli extremist opposed to the Oslo Accords peace process with the Palestinians.

Rabin was shot at the conclusion of a peace rally attended by over one hundred thousand supporters of the Oslo process in Tel Aviv, Israel. Amir was a right-wing law student and member of the Kahanist movement, opposed to territorial concessions to Palestinians. He fired at point-blank range, and Rabin died at Ichilov Hospital within hours. The assassination shocked Israel—memorial sites filled with mourners, and the event was termed sikat Rabin, or the Rabin assassination.

Rabin and Foreign Minister Shimon Peres had negotiated the Oslo Accords in 1993, establishing the foundation for Palestinian self-government and a two-state solution. Right-wing Israeli opponents viewed the Oslo process as a betrayal of Jewish territorial claims in the West Bank and Gaza. Rabin had received death threats from extremists, and some Israeli political figures had used inflammatory rhetoric depicting him as a traitor.

Amir was arrested, tried, and sentenced to life imprisonment, where he remains incarcerated. Rabin's death was mourned internationally as the loss of a statesman willing to compromise. President Bill Clinton eulogized him. Yet the assassination demoralized the Israeli left and emboldened the right. Subsequent elections brought right-wing government back to power. The Oslo peace process stalled and eventually collapsed, and no two-state solution has been achieved in the decades since Rabin's death.

Rabin's assassination stands as a singular moment in Middle Eastern history: a leader making a historic compromise for peace was killed by his own countrymen for that very compromise. The event shattered the mythology of Israeli unity and exposed the depth of political division over the question of territory and coexistence. Unlike many assassinations driven by external forces, Amir's act was rooted entirely in internal Israeli politics—in the struggle between two competing visions of the Israeli state. The assassination did not prevent the peace process immediately, but it marked its symbolic end and became the hinge point after which the Israeli-Palestinian conflict entered a new, more violent phase.
